signals.title: @elenaantoniou3: The core of the broken pledge lies in a promise made during Google's 2014 acquisition of DeepMind, and a series of events that dismantled it
signals.content: The core of the broken pledge lies in a promise made during Google's 2014 acquisition of DeepMind, and a series of events that dismantled it step-by-step. 📜 The 2014 Promise When Google acquired DeepMind for around $400-500 million, it was conditional on an unprecedented, legally binding agreement: an independent ethics board to ensure the AI would never be misused for military purposes. This "Do No Harm" principle was a core condition of the deal. ⚔️ The Two "Drops" The pledge didn't break overnight; it was chipped away in two major moves: · The First Crack (2018: Project Maven): Google allowed its AI to analyze military drone footage. 4,000 employees signed a petition, and Google backed out, formally pledging not to develop AI for weapons or surveillance. · The Point of No Return (2025-2026): Leadership quietly removed the weapons/surveillance ban from the official AI principles. They then signed a classified deal allowing the Pentagon to use Gemini for "any lawful purpose" on secret networks. 💔 The Betrayal and Unionization Staff saw this as a direct betrayal of the 2014 promise. Fearing their AI could enable "lethal autonomous weapons and mass surveillance," over 600 employees signed an open letter and launched a unionization drive to force an ethics oversight body. So, the original promise did exist, but the same company that made it eventually prioritized government contracts over the founding principle. The classified nature of the Pentagon deal is a huge part of why employees are so powerless—want me to explain why the "black box" secrecy makes their fears worse?

signals.brief_en: The core of the broken pledge lies in a promise made during Google's 2014 acquisition of DeepMind. The promise included a legally binding agreement for an independent ethics board to ensure AI would not be misused for military purposes. However, this pledge was dismantled through a series of events, including Google's involvement in Project Maven and a classified deal with the Pentagon.

signals.title: @GreatRecall26: They built the targeting system in Israel first. It was called Lavender. Now they're building the infrastructure here. Flock cameras. AI dat
signals.content: They built the targeting system in Israel first. It was called Lavender. Now they're building the infrastructure here. Flock cameras. AI data centers. 20 billion plate scans a month. The architecture is already up. In 2024, reporting by +972 Magazine and The Guardian revealed that the Israeli military used an AI system called Lavender to generate targeting lists — identifying individuals for lethal strikes based on algorithmic analysis of phone data, social connections, and behavioral patterns. A companion system called "Where's Daddy" tracked when targets entered their family homes — so strikes could be carried out there. These weren't rogue programs. They were institutionalized. Documented. Defended. The AI didn't confirm guilt. It generated probability scores. Human review, according to reporting, was often cursory — sometimes as little as 20 seconds per target. The algorithm decided. People died. Over 40,000 confirmed killed in Gaza per figures used by the United Nations. Over 1.9 million displaced. An entire civilian population living under a system where an algorithm could flag your phone, track your location, and mark your home for a strike. Now look at what's being built here. Flock Safety cameras conduct over 20 billion license plate scans every month across the United States. They track where you go, when you go there, and who you go with. They build a pattern of life — the same data profile that AI targeting systems use to generate threat scores. Cities that tried to cancel their Flock contracts were forced to put trash bags over the cameras. The company retained control of the infrastructure. The Secret Service visited a man because of who followed him on Instagram. Federal agencies have been documented accessing Flock databases in states where that access is explicitly prohibited by law. An American woman was pulled out of her car at gunpoint — twice in one week — because a Flock camera misidentified her vehicle. AI data centers are being built at a pace that has no civilian explanation. The computational capacity being deployed domestically exceeds what streaming, commerce, and consumer AI require. Pattern of life analysis. Behavioral scoring. Social graph mapping. These are not hypothetical future applications. They are the documented present applications of the infrastructure being built right now. The question isn't whether this can happen here. The question is whether you're going to wait until it does. The Reconstitution answers it permanently: Location tracking without your explicit consent = High Treason. Mandatory life imprisonment. Not a fine. Not a civil lawsuit. Not a policy review. Treason. For the executives who authorized it. For the officials who approved the contracts. For everyone in the chain who knew. No AI profiling. No autonomous enforcement of any kind without citizen jury authorization. No algorithm generates a consequence for an American citizen without human beings — your neighbors — reviewing and authorizing it. No Flock cameras. No smart meter surveillance. No biometric collection without consent. Hardcoded. Permanently unamendable. No future Congress, no future emergency, no future administration touches it. When the penalty is mandatory life imprisonment, the business model collapses. You need a legal framework where no rational actor ever installs one without your consent. That framework exists. It's at https://t.co/x09ovOt82Z. Read Article IX.

signals.content: 🤥👁 Space-Eyes deal: enter Trump Jr.? American defense-tech upstart Space-Eyes is merging with SPAC McKinley Acquisition Corp. in a deal that pegs the combined company at $638 million. But the thing is Eric Trump, the US president's son, is significantly upping his stake: he's now the third-largest private shareholder, set to serve as strategic advisor to the new entity, and has a hand in picking the board. There's no word from Trump's team on the terms. Space-Eyes builds AI for geospatial intelligence and drone defense systems like SeaWatch and Morpheus. Its main bread and butter is, thus, government contracts. And that makes this whole arrangement land with a thud.
